title: Forward-testing my MNQ system on live data: 155 trades, +$7,165 at 1 micro, plus how I test before anything goes in
author: JayTheFknSavage
selftext:
https://i.redd.it/59s07vuq292i1.png

I’ve been building a rule-based system for MNQ (Nasdaq micro futures): 16 intraday strategies, no AI making trade decisions. I use Claude to help write and test my own rules, never to pick trades. Here’s where it stands, including the parts that aren’t proven yet.

**How an idea gets in (most don’t):**

* **Pass rule written before results.** If I change the rule after looking, the test doesn’t count.
* **Both eras must agree:** 2011–18 and 2019–26. Plenty of ideas work in one era and die in the other.
* **It must beat a random-entry control** run with the same exits and costs.
* **Cost margin first:** gross edge per trade ÷ cost per trade. Most ideas fail right there. A popular EMA-ribbon setup I tested came out at 0.04× cost.
* I ran an automated search over roughly **430,000 generated strategies. Zero passed.** That one taught me the most.

**Forward results (screenshot):**

* **Live market data since Nov 3:** 155 trades, **+$7,165**, 1 micro per signal, **41.9% winners.** The money comes from winners being bigger than losers, not from the win rate.
* A weekly review grades it automatically, and the rule is **no changes until 60+ live trades**. Every review so far says “no change.”
* **As of today it’s automated through a broker** on a prop-firm eval, which is still sim capital. The first trade was a −$130 stop that filled exactly at its price, matching the backtest.

**What this doesn’t prove yet:**

* Two weeks of forward data is not two years. It shows the process and the plumbing work, not that the edge will last.

I’ll update with the full record, good or bad. Happy to answer questions on the method. I won’t share exact entries.

comments.author: AoideusWasBanned
comments.body: Beating a random-entry control is the part I like most here, almost nobody does that. How does the 41.9% win rate compare to what the backtest expected for the same kind of days?

replies.author: JayTheFknSavage
replies.body:
Thanks. The random control is the part that killed most of my ideas, so I trust it.

Backtest (2019–26, same 1-micro sizing) expected about **48.6% winners, +$26.7 a trade**. Forward so far is **41.9% winners, but about +$46 a trade**. So it’s winning less often but winning bigger than the backtest.

Two honest reasons for the gap:

1. **A small sample.** At 155 trades, the win rate swings about ±4% just from chance, so 41.9% sits roughly 1.7 standard errors under expected. That’s within normal range, not a red flag yet.
2. **One higher-frequency component ran every day** during the first two weeks, when the backtest only lets it trade on days that pass a morning filter. It made up most of the trades and dragged the win rate down. That’s fixed as of this week, so the next batch should compare more cleanly.

The number I’m watching more than win rate is $ per trade against the backtest, plus drawdown. I’ll post the comparison again at 60+ trades under the corrected setup.

comments.author: RonPosit
comments.body: Massive waste of time. People love pretending a script can bottle up an edge forever while completely ignoring regime changes. The market shifts, the parameters break, and then they spend months "re-optimizing" for a market that's already moved on. You can't automate timing when the underlying conditions never stay the same.

replies.author: JayTheFknSavage
replies.body:
Fair point. Regime change is what kills most scripts, and that’s exactly why I built mine to be tested against it instead of fitted to one market.

* **Every rule has to work in two different eras:** 2011–18 (low vol, slow grind) and 2019–26 (COVID, 2022 bear, AI run). If it only works in one, it’s dead.
* **Parameters are frozen after the test.** No re-optimizing. Most of my “improvements” fail the random control and never ship. I killed another one tonight.
* **The tuning-forever problem is real**, so instead of re-optimizing, the forward check just asks: is live still matching the backtest? If live drifts outside what the backtest expects, it gets flagged and I stop it. I don’t retune it.
* **I track the regime** (calm / normal / lively / wild) so I know which conditions a result came from.

You can’t automate timing perfectly, agreed. The goal isn’t a forever edge. It’s knowing quickly when the edge stops showing up.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Writing the pass rule before seeing results and testing against random entries are the habits that matter most, so that's a solid process. Your own caveat is the key one. A profit factor that high after about two weeks usually settles lower once more trades come in, so I wouldn't judge the edge by it yet. One thing I'd add is to write down now what counts as "off track," such as a drawdown size or a profit factor floor, so the weekly review can fail. If you want another check on the history side, Cymetica's Backtest Labs holds out the last part of the data, which is useful for a second look.

replies.author: JayTheFknSavage
replies.body:
Thank you and that’s a fair point, and I’m with you on not judging a PF from two weeks of trades.

The off-track line is already written down. The weekly review checks the forward results against two tripwires set before the forward test started:

* **a drawdown limit:** if the forward drawdown goes past roughly the backtest’s worst-case range, it fails.
* **a losing-streak limit:** if the run of losing trades gets longer than the backtest ever produced, it fails.

If either one trips, the system gets pulled for review, not retuned. Below that, it’s just noise and I leave it alone.

On the history side, I already split it: every rule gets picked on 2011–18 and has to hold up on 2019–26, which it never saw. Anything that only works in one era gets thrown out. That held-out era is the second look you’re describing.
